The study examines Veech groups of origamis, or square-tiled translation surfaces, as a systematic source of finite-index subgroups of \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\). An origami is obtained by gluing finitely many unit squares along parallel edges; equivalently, it is a finite cover of the flat torus branched over at most one point. Because of this arithmetic structure, the derivatives of orientation-preserving affine automorphisms of an origami form a finite-index subgroup of \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\), called its Veech group. This makes origamis especially suitable for studying the distinction between congruence and noncongruence subgroups.

The work develops constructions that produce decreasing sequences of Veech groups. By modifying the covering data of an origami while controlling its affine symmetries, one obtains surfaces whose Veech groups form nested finite-index subgroups of the modular group. The associated permutation representations and cylinder decompositions provide concrete tools for identifying these groups, computing their indices, and determining which matrices can occur as derivatives of affine automorphisms.

Particular attention is given to origamis of genus \(2\), where explicit examples make the noncongruence phenomenon visible. Their Veech groups are analyzed using group-theoretic and geometric information, including parabolic elements arising from cylinder decompositions. The resulting cusp data and level information can then be compared with the restrictions satisfied by congruence subgroups. These comparisons show that the Veech groups in question cannot contain any principal congruence subgroup of the required level and therefore are genuinely noncongruence subgroups of \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\).

The genus-\(2\) constructions serve as the basis for a broader existence argument. Through suitable origami and covering constructions, the examples can be extended while increasing the genus and preserving the obstruction to congruence. Consequently, noncongruence Veech groups are not confined to isolated low-genus surfaces. The main result proves that for every integer \(g>1\), there exists a translation surface of genus \(g\) whose Veech group is a noncongruence subgroup of \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\). Thus, noncongruence behavior occurs in every higher genus and forms a general feature of the arithmetic and geometric theory of translation surfaces.

## Veech Surfaces and Teichmüller Theory

William Veech made fundamental contributions to the study of translation surfaces and Teichmüller dynamics. A **translation surface** is a geometric surface constructed by gluing polygons along parallel sides. Straight-line motion on such a surface provides a mathematical model for billiard trajectories in rational polygons.

A **Veech surface** is a translation surface whose group of affine symmetries—called the Veech group—is a lattice in \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})\). These surfaces exhibit a remarkable property known as the **Veech dichotomy**: in any given direction, the straight-line flow is either completely periodic or uniquely ergodic. Thus, trajectories are either organized into cylinders of closed paths or become uniformly distributed across the surface.

Veech surfaces also generate special curves in **Teichmueller space**, known as Teichmueller curves. These curves are closed orbits of the natural \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})\) action on the moduli space of translation surfaces. They connect geometry, topology, dynamical systems, and number theory.

The relationship between Veech surfaces and Teichmueller theory has become central to modern research. It provides powerful tools for understanding polygonal billiards, interval exchange transformations, moduli spaces, and the long-term behavior of dynamical systems.

counterfactuals.output:
### Summary

Square-tiled surfaces, also called origamis, provide a combinatorial method for constructing translation surfaces whose Veech groups are finite-index subgroups of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\). A square-tiled surface is obtained by gluing finitely many unit squares along parallel edges by translations. It can be encoded by two permutations \(h\) and \(v\), describing the horizontal and vertical gluings. The subgroup \(\langle h,v\rangle\) must act transitively for the surface to be connected, while the cycle structure of the commutator
\[
[h,v]=hvh^{-1}v^{-1}
\]
determines the ramification over the torus and hence the genus through the Riemann–Hurwitz formula.

The affine symmetry group of such a surface acts by derivatives in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\). Its image, the Veech group \(\Gamma(X)\), is the stabilizer of the corresponding origami under the natural \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\)-action. Because an origami is a finite cover of the square torus branched over at most one point, \(\Gamma(X)\) always has finite index in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\). Square-tiled surfaces therefore reduce the problem of constructing noncongruence Veech groups to the explicit construction of finite combinatorial covers whose stabilizers are noncongruence subgroups.

For every genus \(g>1\), one chooses gluing permutations whose commutator has total ramification defect \(2g-2\). This fixes the genus while leaving enough freedom to alter the horizontal and vertical cylinder decompositions. The widths of these cylinders determine parabolic elements of the Veech group and, equivalently, the cusp widths of the associated finite-index subgroup. By arranging the square gluings appropriately, one obtains a family \(X_g\) with computable cusp widths and a computable \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\)-orbit.

Noncongruence is then proved using a level obstruction. Let
\[
N=\operatorname{lcm}\{\text{cusp widths of }\Gamma(X_g)\}.
\]
Wohlfahrt’s theorem implies that if \(\Gamma(X_g)\) were a congruence subgroup, its congruence level would have to equal \(N\), up to the standard convention concerning \(-I\). The combinatorial origami action allows one to test membership of generators and words explicitly. One then shows either that the principal congruence subgroup \(\Gamma(N)\) is not contained in \(\Gamma(X_g)\), or that the index and reduction of \(\Gamma(X_g)\) modulo \(N\) are incompatible with those of any congruence subgroup of level \(N\). Thus \(\Gamma(X_g)\) is a finite-index subgroup of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) that is not defined by congruence conditions.

The construction works uniformly in genus because the genus can be increased by inserting additional squares or ramification blocks without destroying the cusp-width obstruction. The resulting theorem is that, for every \(g>1\), there exists a connected square-tiled surface of genus \(g\) whose Veech group is noncongruence. This demonstrates that noncongruence behavior is not exceptional or confined to low genus: it occurs throughout the moduli spaces of translation surfaces and can be produced by explicit finite permutation data.
